title: The Ruy López
standfirst: Named for a Spanish priest who wrote it down in 1561 and still the main battleground of 1.e4 e5. Nothing here happens fast — that's the point.

steps.title: Pressure, not threats
body: The Italian aims a bishop at f7 and asks a direct question. The Ruy López asks a slower one: it attacks the defender of Black's centre and then does nothing about it for ten moves.
Grandmasters call the resulting squeeze “Spanish torture”. Watch how little actually happens, and how uncomfortable it becomes anyway.

steps.title: The usual first move
body: Same start as the Italian — a pawn to the centre, two pieces freed behind it.

steps.title: Black claims his share
body: Symmetry again. Everything that follows is about who gets to break it first.

steps.title: Develop with a question
body: The knight develops and attacks e5. Black must answer it before doing anything else.

steps.title: The natural defender
body: The knight defends e5 and develops. Note what is holding Black's centre together — it's this piece, and White's next move is about it.

steps.title: Attack the defender, not the pawn
body: This is the Ruy López. The bishop doesn't attack e5 — it attacks the knight that defends e5. Remove or distract that knight and the pawn falls.
It looks like a pin, and beginners often assume e5 is already hanging. It isn't yet: 4.Bxc6 dxc6 5.Nxe5 Qd4 wins the piece back. The pressure is real but indirect.

steps.title: The Morphy Defence
body: Black asks the bishop to decide: retreat, or take on c6 and give up the bishop pair. Named for Paul Morphy, and played in the overwhelming majority of games.
Asking a question costs a tempo. It's worth it because it forces White to commit.

steps.title: Keep the bishop, keep the tension
body: White declines to trade. The bishop stays on the a4–e8 diagonal, still eyeing c6 from a distance, and the threat to win e5 is still notional rather than immediate.

steps.title: Hit something back
body: Black develops the last kingside knight and attacks e4. Every developing move should carry a question if it can.

steps.title: Castling into a “hanging” pawn
body: White ignores the attack on e4 and castles. If 5…Nxe4 6.d4 hits the knight and reopens everything, and Black's extra pawn is temporary.
Development beats material in the first ten moves. That's the whole justification for this move.

steps.title: The quiet square
body: Not to c5, where the Italian bishop goes — here it just guards the knight and clears the way to castle. Modest moves are normal in the Ruy.

steps.title: Now e4 is properly defended
body: The rook backs up the e-pawn, and the earlier bluff becomes a genuine threat: Bxc6 followed by Nxe5 is suddenly real.

steps.title: Shutting the door
body: Black finally kicks the bishop off the dangerous diagonal, gaining queenside space in the process. It also loosens Black's own pawns — every gain of space costs something.

steps.title: The bishop finds its home
body: It looks like a retreat but the bishop now stares at f7 along a diagonal that will matter for the rest of the game. It often sits here for twenty moves.

steps.title: The Closed Ruy López
body: Black shores up e5 and opens the c8 bishop. This position has been reached in tens of thousands of master games — it's a starting point, not an ending.

White's long-term plan is c3 and d4 to build the big centre, then the knight tour Nbd2–f1–g3. Black plays for …Na5 hitting the b3 bishop, or …Bg4 pinning the f3 knight. Nobody is attacking anybody yet.
